etymology: From Old Norse klippa (to cut, to clip); the past tense appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Jeremiah's oracle of mourning over Moab.
biblical_def:
For every head shall be bald, and every beard clipped.

Clipped appears once in the Authorized Version, in Jeremiah's extended oracle against Moab (Jeremiah 48), describing signs of mourning — baldness and a shorn or clipped beard — that would mark the nation in the day of its judgment. Shaving the head and trimming or cutting the beard were recognized ancient Near Eastern mourning practices, sometimes performed in pagan ritual excess that Israel's own law explicitly forbade its priests and people (Lev 21:5, Deu 14:1), but here appearing as the natural, universal human response to catastrophic loss rather than a prescribed ritual. Moab's judgment is described with unusual pathos for an oracle against a foreign nation — my heart shall mourn for the men of Kirheres (Jer 48:31), the LORD's own grief mingled with the sentence He pronounces, a pattern seen elsewhere in the prophets where judgment on the nations is never gleeful but sorrowful, even as it remains just and necessary. Moab's specific sin named through the chapter is pride: we have heard the pride of Moab, (he is exceeding proud) his loftiness, and his arrogancy, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart (Jer 48:29), the same root sin Scripture consistently names as precipitating judgment on nations and individuals alike, from Babel to Babylon to every proud heart since.

CLIPPED, v. Past tense and participle: cut short, trimmed away.

corruption_summary: A reading of prophetic judgment oracles as merely gleeful condemnation of foreign enemies misses the genuine sorrow woven through this very chapter, where the LORD's own heart mourns even the judgment He justly pronounces.
corruption_paragraphs: It is possible to read oracles against the nations as tribal triumphalism, cheering an enemy's downfall; Jeremiah 48:31 specifically denies this reading, recording the LORD's own grief for Moab even as judgment falls.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the oracle's own balance: judgment against pride is just and certain, yet God takes no delight in the destruction of the wicked (cf. Eze 33:11), a sorrow that should temper how His people regard even deserved judgment on others.

etymology: From Old French clos, from Latin clausus (closed, shut), the comparative form; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Proverbs' teaching on the difference between true friendship and mere acquaintance.
biblical_def:
There is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.

Closer appears once in the Authorized Version, in one of Proverbs' most quoted sayings on friendship, distinguishing between the man that hath friends, who must shew himself friendly to keep them, and a rarer thing altogether: a friend that sticketh closer than a brother (Pro 18:24). The proverb draws its force from the strongest natural bond ancient Israel recognized, brotherhood, and names something even more durable and reliable — a friendship of loyalty proven, not merely inherited by blood, that outlasts even family ties in its steadfastness. The book of Proverbs elsewhere fills out what such friendship looks like in practice: faithful are the wounds of a friend (Pro 27:6), a friend loveth at all times (Pro 17:17), iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend (Pro 27:17) — a portrait of friendship as costly loyalty, honest correction, and mutual strengthening rather than mere pleasant company. Christian tradition has long read this proverb as ultimately finding its fullest referent in Christ Himself, the friend who called His disciples friends rather than servants (Joh 15:15) and who defined the greatest love as a man laying down his life for his friends (Joh 15:13), sticking closer than any brother by nature could.

webster_full: CLOSE, adj. Near; intimate; adhering firmly.
CLOSER, adj. The comparative degree: nearer or more intimate than another thing compared.

corruption_summary: A culture of wide but shallow social connection can mistake the number of acquaintances for the presence of true friendship, missing Proverbs' own distinction between a man who merely hath friends and the rarer friend who sticks closer than a brother.
corruption_paragraphs: Social platforms measure friendship by breadth of connection, a metric Proverbs itself already anticipates and corrects: many acquaintances are easily gained, but the friend who sticks closer than a brother is proven only through costly, faithful loyalty over time.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ's own fulfillment of this proverb: greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends (Joh 15:13), the standard by which every lesser friendship is finally measured.

etymology: From Old French conforter (to strengthen greatly), from Latin confortare; the archaic second-person singular past tense ("thou comfortedst") appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Isaiah's short psalm of thanksgiving.
biblical_def:
Though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me.

Comfortedst appears once in the Authorized Version, in Isaiah 12, a brief psalm of praise placed immediately after the great oracles of judgment and the promised virgin-born child of Isaiah 7-11, functioning as the fitting response once salvation has come: O LORD, I will praise thee: though thou wast angry with me, thine anger is turned away, and thou comfortedst me. The verse holds both realities together without softening either: real divine anger, justly provoked, and real divine comfort, freely given once that anger is turned away — not by pretending the anger was never deserved, but by the LORD Himself accomplishing the turning. The psalm continues in words later echoed throughout redemptive history: behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and not be afraid: for the LORD JEHOVAH is my strength and my song; he also is become my salvation (Isa 12:2), language the New Testament applies directly to the joy of gospel salvation, drawing water out of the wells of salvation (Isa 12:3) becoming an image used at the Feast of Tabernacles and taken up by Christ Himself when he stood and cried, saying, If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink (Joh 7:37-38).

webster_full: COMFORT, v.t. To strengthen the mind under affliction; to console; to give solace.
COMFORTEDST, v. Archaic second-person singular past tense: thou didst comfort.

corruption_paragraphs: A theology built only on divine comfort, without divine anger against sin first justly provoked, cannot account for what this psalm actually says; the comfort is meaningful precisely because the anger was real and the turning was God's own gracious act, not a denial that anger was ever warranted.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the psalm's own sequence: wrath justly kindled, wrath graciously turned, comfort freely given, and praise the only fitting response, a pattern fulfilled in the gospel Christ Himself invoked at the Feast of Tabernacles (Joh 7:37-38).

etymology: From Old English cuman (to come), the plural noun form; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Ezekiel's vision of the pattern of the temple shown to a repentant, exiled people.
biblical_def:
The goings out thereof, and the comings in thereof, and all the forms thereof.

Comings appears once in the Authorized Version, paired with goings out, in Ezekiel's detailed vision of a future temple shown to the prophet while in exile in Babylon, a vision he is commanded to show the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities: and let them measure the pattern (Eze 43:10). The comings in and goings out name the entrances, exits, and overall layout of the temple's design, a pattern given in exhaustive, architectural detail across Ezekiel 40-48, functioning not as a mere building project but as a comprehensive theological statement to a defeated, exiled people that God's purposes for His dwelling among them were not finished. The instruction that this measured pattern should produce shame at Israel's iniquities, rather than mere architectural interest, shows the vision's true aim: renewed covenant seriousness, a people who would keep the whole form thereof, and all the ordinances thereof, and do them (Eze 43:11) once restored. The vision culminates in the return of the glory of the LORD to this temple (Eze 43:1-5), the same glory that had departed in judgment earlier in the book (Eze 10:18-19), a promise of restored presence that finds its ultimate fulfillment not in a rebuilt physical structure but in Christ Himself, Emmanuel, God with us (Mat 1:23).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the passage's own logic: a vision of restored divine presence is meant to provoke, not idle curiosity, but shame over sin and renewed resolve to keep God's ordinances, exactly the response Ezekiel is told to seek.

etymology: From Latin commodus (fit, convenient, suitable), through French commode; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Luke's account of Paul's hazardous sea voyage to Rome.
biblical_def:
Because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence.

Commodious appears once in the Authorized Version, in Luke's detailed, eyewitness account of Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner, describing the harbor of Fair Havens in Crete as not commodious, not suitable or convenient, for wintering the ship (Act 27:12). The practical decision that followed — sailing on toward a better harbor rather than remaining in an inadequate one — proved disastrous, as Luke records in careful nautical detail the violent tempestuous wind called Euroclydon that drove the ship for fourteen days before it finally ran aground and broke apart near Malta (Act 27:14-44). Paul had specifically warned against this decision, perceiving that this voyage will be with hurt and much damage (Act 27:10), a warning the centurion and shipmaster overruled in favor of the majority's judgment about the more commodious harbor. Yet the LORD had already promised Paul, through an angel that stood by him that night, that he must be brought before Caesar, and lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee (Act 27:23-24), a promise fulfilled exactly, every soul aboard surviving the wreck as foretold, demonstrating that God's providence secures His purposes even through, not merely despite, human misjudgment and genuine disaster.

COMMODIOUS, adj. Roomy; spacious; well adapted to its purpose.

corruption_summary: A fatalistic misreading could conclude that since God's promise was kept anyway, the majority's poor decision to sail did not matter, missing that Scripture holds both real human responsibility for bad judgment and God's sovereign faithfulness together without excusing the former.
corruption_paragraphs: The fact that God kept His promise to Paul despite the shipwreck does not erase the text's own verdict on the decision: Paul had rightly perceived the danger, and the majority's judgment, however reasonable it seemed, proved wrong and costly.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the whole episode's demonstration of providence: God's purposes for Paul stood secure not because the voyage went smoothly but precisely through the storm and wreck, 'God hath given thee all them that sail with thee' (Act 27:24) fulfilled exactly as spoken.

etymology: A compound of common and wealth (weal, well-being), from Old English commun and wela; appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's description of the Gentiles' former standing before Christ.
biblical_def:
Being aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise.

Commonwealth appears once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's letter to the Ephesians, describing what Gentile believers had been before their union with Christ: aliens from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers from the covenants of promise, having no hope, and without God in the world (Eph 2:12). The word names Israel's whole covenant polity — its citizenship, its promises, its access to God through the appointed means He had given — from which Gentiles by birth stood entirely excluded, outsiders to a national and spiritual body they had no natural claim upon. Paul's point is not to dwell on that former exclusion but to magnify the reversal Christ accomplished: but now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ (Eph 2:13), breaking down the middle wall of partition (Eph 2:14) so completely that Gentile believers are no more strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God (Eph 2:19). The passage stands as one of the New Testament's clearest statements that the church is not a replacement commonwealth built from scratch but the same covenant people of God now opened, in Christ, to Jew and Gentile alike, one new man, so making peace (Eph 2:15).

etymology: From Latin compactus, past participle of compingere (to fasten together, to join); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in the Psalmist's celebration of Jerusalem's unity as pilgrims arrive for the feasts.
biblical_def:
Jerusalem is builded as a city that is compact together.

Compact appears once in the Authorized Version, in Psalm 122, one of the Songs of Degrees sung by pilgrims ascending to Jerusalem for the appointed feasts, describing the city as builded as a city that is compact together — closely joined, unified, its houses and walls forming one coherent whole rather than a scattered collection of separate settlements. The psalm opens with the pilgrim's own joy at the prospect of arrival, I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD (Psa 122:1), and the compactness of the city becomes an image for something deeper than architecture: whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, unto the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the LORD (Psa 122:4), Israel's twelve tribes unified in common worship at one appointed place. The psalm's closing prayer, pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee (Psa 122:6), extends the theme of compactness into covenant solidarity, a city whose physical unity mirrors the spiritual unity of a people gathered to worship one God at one place, a pattern the New Testament applies to the church itself, built together for an habitation of God through the Spirit (Eph 2:22), living stones... built up a spiritual house (1Pe 2:5).

etymology: From Latin compactus, past participle of compingere (to fasten together, to join); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Paul's teaching on the growth of the body of Christ.
biblical_def:
The whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth.

Compacted appears once in the Authorized Version, in Ephesians 4, Paul's description of the church as a body whose growth and health depend on every part functioning together, fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part (Eph 4:16). The image builds on Paul's fuller teaching of the body just given, that Christ gave gifted men — apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers — for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ (Eph 4:11-12), so that the whole structure's soundness depends not on a few prominent members but on every joint supplying its measure of strength to the compacted, unified whole. The stated goal of this growth is maturity and doctrinal stability: that we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine (Eph 4:14), a church so well-joined and compacted that false teaching cannot easily dislodge individual members from the body's collective strength. The image stands against both isolated individualism, which forgets that every believer is a joint supplying necessary strength, and passive spectatorship, which leaves the compacting work to a few while most members contribute nothing to the body's health.

etymology: From Latin comparabilis, from comparare (to pair, to match); appearing once in the Authorized Version, in Jeremiah's Lamentations over the fall of Jerusalem.
biblical_def:
The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers.

Comparable appears once in the Authorized Version, in Lamentations, Jeremiah's grief-stricken poem over Jerusalem's fall to Babylon, describing the reversal that had overtaken the city's own sons: the precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter! (Lam 4:2). The image is one of catastrophic devaluation — men once precious, valuable as gold, now treated as common, breakable clay pottery, worthless and disposable, a picture matching the siege's actual horrors described immediately after, including the unthinkable famine that drove even the pitiful mothers to cook their own children (Lam 4:10). Lamentations as a whole refuses to look away from judgment's full weight, written as five careful acrostic poems that impose form and structure on grief too large to express formlessly, yet the book does not end in despair: it is of the LORD's mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness (Lam 3:22-23), one of Scripture's most quoted affirmations of hope, arising not despite the devastation surrounding the comparable-to-gold sons reduced to earthen pitchers, but directly out of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from COMPARE: capable of being likened to or matched with; here of Jerusalem's sons, once comparable to fine gold, degraded to the worth of common clay pottery in siege and judgment.
webster_full: COMPARE, v.t. To examine the relation of one thing to another; to liken.
COMPARABLE, adj. Worthy of comparison; capable of being likened to.
In Lamentations 4:2 the word measures Jerusalem's precious sons against fine gold, now debased.
The image pictures catastrophic devaluation under the horrors of Babylon's siege (Lam 4:1-10).
The book turns to hope in Lamentations 3:22-23: 'his compassions fail not... great is thy faithfulness.'
scriptures: Lam 4:2
The precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, how are they esteemed as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter!
corruption_summary: A sanitized approach to lament that skips quickly past real grief to premature comfort misses the pattern Lamentations itself models, which dwells honestly in devastation for chapters before its hope is earned, not asserted lightly.
corruption_paragraphs: A rush to resolve grief too quickly can bypass the honest, structured mourning Lamentations practices across its five careful poems, mourning that takes the fallen city's true horror seriously before any word of hope is spoken.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Lamentations' own pattern: hope that has passed through, not around, real devastation, arriving at 'great is thy faithfulness' (Lam 3:23) only after chapters that refuse to look away from what judgment actually cost.
roots_summary: Comparable occurs once, in Lamentations' image of Jerusalem's sons debased from gold to worthless clay, part of the book's honest, structured mourning over the city's fall that nonetheless arrives at one of Scripture's clearest affirmations of God's faithfulness.

The image belongs to Lamentations' unflinching description of siege and judgment (Lam 4:1-10).
The book is structured as five careful acrostic poems, giving form to grief rather than suppressing it.
Lamentations 3:22-23 turns to hope: 'his compassions fail not... great is thy faithfulness.'
The hope arrives only after honest mourning, not as a substitute for it.

etymology: From Latin componere (to put together), through Old French compondre; appearing once in the Authorized Version as an adjective/noun, in the recipe God gives Moses for the tabernacle's anointing oil.
biblical_def:
An oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary.

Compound appears once in the Authorized Version, in Exodus 30's detailed recipe for the holy anointing oil, made an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary from pure myrrh, sweet cinnamon, sweet calamus, cassia, and olive oil, mixed by a skilled perfumer's craft into a single, specifically formulated blend set apart entirely for sacred use (Exo 30:23-25). The command that immediately follows is severe in its exclusivity: this oil was to anoint the tabernacle, the ark, the altar, and Aaron and his sons for the priesthood, and upon man's flesh shall it not be poured, neither shall ye make any other like it, after the composition of it (Exo 30:32) — a formula so holy that reproducing it for common or personal use carried the penalty of being cut off from his people (Exo 30:33). This severity teaches a consistent biblical principle: holiness is not a vague quality attached loosely to religious things but a specific, God-defined set-apartness that human ingenuity may not casually imitate or commercialize for its own purposes. The anointing oil's exclusive use on priests, tabernacle furniture, and consecrated objects prefigures the far greater anointing of Christ Himself, whose very title means Anointed One, and the Spirit given to Him without measure (Joh 3:34), the true and final fulfillment of every drop of oil compounded according to this ancient, guarded recipe.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from COMPOUND: to mix or combine ingredients into one substance; here as a noun/adjective of the specially formulated holy anointing oil, its composition forbidden to common use.
webster_full: COMPOUND, v.t. To mix or combine, as ingredients into one substance.
COMPOUND, n. or adj. A substance formed by combining separate ingredients according to a set formula.
In Exodus 30:25 the word names the specially formulated holy anointing oil, made 'after the art of the apothecary.'
The oil anointed the tabernacle, its furniture, and Aaron's priestly line exclusively (Exo 30:26-30).
Reproducing the formula for common use carried the penalty of being 'cut off from his people' (Exo 30:33).
scriptures: And thou shalt make it an oil of holy ointment, an ointment compound after the art of the apothecary: it shall be an holy anointing oil.
corruption_summary: A vague, generalized notion that treats any religious-feeling object or ritual as equally holy misses the precise, exclusive, God-defined set-apartness the anointing oil's strict formula and forbidden imitation were meant to teach.
corruption_paragraphs: A diffuse spirituality that calls almost anything sacred, provided it feels meaningful, loses the sharp edge this text insists on: holiness here is a specific, guarded formula, not a loose category anyone may claim or replicate for their own purposes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the type's fulfillment in Christ: every drop of this guarded, exclusive oil pointed toward the one true Anointed One, upon whom the Spirit rests without measure (Joh 3:34), the reality no imitation formula could ever produce.
